evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §15 l.350-351: "`bound_at`, written by `tp init --epic` and `tp set --epic <id>`, rewritten when the file is bound to another epic"; §17 l.412-413: "A file bound before this release has no `bound_at`, and the chart shows its binding time as unknown for that epic, never placing it on a guessed day." Counterexample: legacy file bound to E1 (no bound_at); `tp set --epic E1` → reading A writes bound_at=now (chart shows binding today), reading B leaves it absent (chart shows unknown).
finding: Whether `tp set --epic <id>` writes `bound_at` when the file is already bound to that same epic is read two ways, and one reading contradicts §17. §15 says bound_at is 'written by ... `tp set --epic <id>`' (every call) and also 'rewritten when the file is bound to another epic' (only on change). On a file bound before this release, re-running `tp set --epic E1` under the first reading stamps today's time as bound_at, which places the binding on a guessed day — exactly what §17 forbids; under the second reading it is a no-op and the time stays unknown. Two implementations' tests disagree on that file.

resolved.evidence: §15: bound_at is written by tp init --epic and only by a tp set --epic <id> that changes the file's epic; re-binding the same epic writes nothing, so a legacy file keeps an unknown binding time (§17).

suggestion: State that `tp set --epic <id>` naming the epic the file is already bound to leaves `bound_at` as it is (absent stays absent); it is written only when the file goes from unbound or another epic to <id>.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §2 line 51: "The server re-derives its data on a fixed tick, hashes the result, and pushes it to the page ... only when the hash changed"; line 58-59: "Its data is the payload of `tp epic export`"; line 61-62: "`tp epic export` gains ... `revision` (a hash of the payload's inputs) and `generated_at`"; line 76-77 acceptance: "an unchanged repository pushes nothing after the first state".
finding: `generated_at` is a per-call timestamp added to the payload the server hashes to decide whether to push. If the hash covers it, every tick changes the hash and the server pushes on every tick, contradicting the acceptance that an unchanged repository pushes nothing. If the hash excludes it, the hash duplicates `revision`. Either way `generated_at` feeds no decision an agent or the page makes: `revision` already answers 'did anything change'.

resolved.evidence: §2: the push decision now reads 'pushes ... only when its revision changed' instead of hashing the whole result, so generated_at (operator-decided in dashboard.md §6 q7) no longer drives pushes.

suggestion: Drop `generated_at` from the export and make the push decision compare `revision` alone. That deletes one key, and the change check exists only once.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §9 lines 212-216: "the longest chain of openings is the main lane, milestones that open beside it in the same column are parallel lanes, milestones with an empty `opens_after` (opened by their own trigger) sit in a lane of their own, and milestones nothing on the main chain waits for form a side lane." vs acceptance line 234: "In a graph where two milestones have an empty `opens_after`, both are placed in the triggered lane." Counterexample: opens_after {M1: [], M2: [M1], M3: [M2], T: []}: the longest chain M1->M2->M3 makes M1 main lane, while the acceptance puts M1 (empty opens_after) in the triggered lane. skills/tp/REFERENCE.md line 1631-1632: "a track's first milestone without an entry opens after none and is always open, as is one whose entry is `[]`."
finding: The lane rules do not partition the milestones, so one milestone can belong to two lanes and the acceptance forces an outcome the main-lane rule forbids. The main chain of openings must start at a milestone that opens after nothing; REFERENCE.md says a track's first milestone without an entry and one whose entry is `[]` are the same thing (always open). Such a root is both 'the longest chain of openings is the main lane' and 'milestones with an empty opens_after ... sit in a lane of their own'. Likewise a milestone opening beside the main chain in the same column that no main-chain milestone waits for fits both 'parallel lanes' and 'side lane'. Two correct implementations will place these milestones differently.

resolved.evidence: §9: lanes now apply in precedence order — an opens_after entry of [] takes the triggered lane first, and the main/parallel/side rules apply among the rest — so the §9 acceptance (two [] milestones both triggered) holds under one reading.

suggestion: State the lane rules as an ordered classification (e.g. main chain first, then explicit `[]` milestones not on the main chain, then parallel, then side), say whether 'empty opens_after' means an explicit `[]` or the effective empty list, and adjust the acceptance to a graph where the empty-entry milestones are off the main chain.

evidence: §1 l.26-27: "3 with a hint when the repository holds neither an epic graph nor a task file"; §2 l.52-54: "A derivation that fails (a malformed graph or task file) is pushed as tp's error and hint, and the page shows it as a banner over the last good state, greyed."
finding: A repository whose `.tp/epics.json` exists but is malformed at startup has two readings: §1's exit 3 ('holds neither an epic graph nor a task file') or §2's error banner. §2's banner sits 'over the last good state', which does not exist at startup, so one implementation exits 3 and another serves a page with only a banner.

resolved.evidence: §2: the banner sits over the last good state 'when there is one', so a malformed graph at startup serves the page with tp's error banner; §1's exit 3 stays for a repository holding neither file.

suggestion: Say whether a malformed graph or task file at startup serves (banner over an empty page) or exits, and with which code.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §10: 'A rule whose selector names no epic, milestone or tag is a `dangling-reference` ... Writers refuse what the rule forbids, as they refuse every lint error.' internal/engine/epiclint.go:279-320 emits dangling-reference via epicError (error severity). REFERENCE.md 'Exit codes (tp epic)' row 1: 'a write whose after-state adds a lint error'.
finding: A forbidden_edges selector that names no epic, milestone or tag is a `dangling-reference`, which is an error, and 'Writers refuse ... every lint error' in the after-state. So `tp epic remove` of an epic a rule names, or a `tp epic set` that drops the last epic carrying a rule's tag, is refused, and a preventive rule over a tag no epic carries yet cannot exist. The spec states none of this, and the tag case cuts against the rule's purpose of forbidding future edges.
suggestion: Either list the refusal under Consequences (as tag_checks providers already are for remove), or make a tag selector that matches no epic valid, and keep dangling-reference for epic and milestone names only.

evidence: §15 line 351-352: "`imported_at`, written by `tp import` and rewritten by every later import"; §17 line 409-411 stage sources list "`claimed.at`, a bound file's `bound_at`, the first task's `started_at`, `done_at` or `done.at`, and the audit round", with no `imported_at`; §17 line 427-428: "A bound file without `bound_at` that has been imported into shows its epic's binding time as unknown."
finding: `imported_at` is written on every import, `--force` included, and carried in both `tp epic export` and `tp export`. Yet no derivation in the spec names it as an input. §17's lifecycle stages are built from `claimed.at`, `bound_at`, `started_at`, `done_at`/`done.at` and the audit round. §17's acceptance mentions an import only to say it does not stand in for `bound_at`. A field that nothing reads is surface no decision needs.

resolved.evidence: imported_at has readers: §16 tp export carries it per task file, and §13's stepper says what happened in each step, the decompose step being the import; §17's acceptance also reads it. Both times are taken whole from lifecycle-timestamps.md §1.

suggestion: Either drop `imported_at` from this release, or state in one clause the figure it feeds (for example, the decompose step's time in §13's stepper) so the field has a reader.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §16: 'It exits 0; 3 with a hint when no task file is found or one cannot be read; `--list` with no task file prints an empty list and exits 0.' §2: 'A derivation that fails (a malformed graph or task file) is pushed as tp's error and hint, and the page shows it as a banner over the last good state'.
finding: `tp export` exits 3 'when no task file is found or one cannot be read', and `--list` with no task file exits 0 with an empty list. The spec does not say what `--list` does when one of many task files is malformed: exit 3 for the whole list, or a row that carries the error. The Specs tab draws `--list` (§12), and §2 turns a failed derivation into a banner over the last good state. Under the exit-3 reading, one bad task file freezes every other spec's row.

resolved.evidence: §16: exit 3 is narrowed to the one file the single-file form reads; --list keeps every readable row beside an unreadable file's row, which carries the error.

suggestion: State `--list`'s behaviour for an unreadable file: a row with its error and the other rows intact (exit 0 or 1), or a whole-command exit 3.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §17: 'work epics per stage (planned, claimed, specced, in progress, done) per day, from the times tp records — `claimed.at`, a bound file's `bound_at`, the first task's `started_at`, `done_at` or `done.at`, and the audit round that brought the last bound file to release.'
finding: Five time sources are listed for four timed stages (planned has none), with no mapping. 'done_at or done.at' and 'the audit round that brought the last bound file to release' both compete for 'done'. The spec does not say which one wins when an epic's `done.at` and its last bound file's release-closing audit round fall on different days, or whether 'done_at' is a task field or an epic field. Two implementations would place the same epic on different days.

resolved.evidence: §17: each stage now names its time — claimed.at dates claimed, the earliest bound_at of its bound files specced, the earliest started_at of their tasks in progress, and the export's done_at (done record or the release-closing audit round, as epicderive.go already derives it) done.

suggestion: Give one source per stage, with the precedence for done: for example, `done.at` when the epic is marked done, else the release-closing audit round. Say whose field `done_at` is.

evidence: §17 l.408-411: "work epics per stage (planned, claimed, specced, in progress, done) per day, from the times tp records — `claimed.at`, a bound file's `bound_at`, the first task's `started_at`, `done_at` or `done.at`, and the audit round that brought the last bound file to release." §4 l.107-108 allows an epic several "bound specs".
finding: The mapping from recorded times to the five stages is not stated, and it is read two ways for 'done' and for epics with several bound files. Five sources are listed (claimed.at, bound_at, first task started_at, done_at/done.at, the audit round bringing the last bound file to release) for four transitions; one implementation dates 'done' by the epic's done record, another by the release audit round, and their day counts differ when the two fall on different days. With several bound files, 'a bound file's bound_at' and 'the first task's started_at' do not say earliest across files or by file order.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 7 (§17 stage-time mapping), fixed by the same repair.

suggestion: Name each stage's entry time: claimed = claimed.at, specced = earliest bound_at over its bound files, in progress = earliest started_at over their tasks, done = the epic's done record (and say what the release audit round is used for, or drop it).

evidence: §17 lines 408-411: "work epics per stage (planned, claimed, specced, in progress, done) per day, from the times tp records — `claimed.at`, a bound file's `bound_at`, the first task's `started_at`, `done_at` or `done.at`, and the audit round that brought the last bound file to release."
finding: The times feeding the five stages are listed without saying which time marks which stage. Four times are given for four timed stages plus an extra one: `done_at or done.at` and 'the audit round that brought the last bound file to release' are both candidates for the done stage, and `done_at` could be a task's or the epic's. An epic with bound files whose last file released but that carries no `done` record (or the reverse) gets a different done day depending on the reading.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 7 (§17 stage-time mapping), fixed by the same repair.

suggestion: Map each stage to its time explicitly (claimed <- claimed.at, specced <- bound_at, in progress <- first task started_at, done <- ...), and say which wins when both done candidates exist.

evidence: §17 l.416-418: "what changed since this browser last saw the page ... compares the payload it stored with the current one"; acceptance l.429: "After a task closes in another terminal, a reload shows it in the strip"; §2 l.51-52: the server pushes each changed state to an open page.
finding: When the browser's stored payload is replaced is unstated, and the acceptance depends on it. If the page stores each pushed payload, a task closed while the page is open updates the baseline through the push and a reload then shows nothing in the strip; if it stores only on load/leave, the reload shows the task. Both read 'since this browser last saw the page', and the acceptance 'After a task closes in another terminal, a reload shows it in the strip' passes for one and fails for the other.

resolved.evidence: §17: the strip's baseline is replaced on load only: each load compares the payload stored at the previous load with the current one, then stores the current one; a push does not move it.

suggestion: State when the baseline is written (e.g. when the page is hidden or closed, never on a live push), and whether the acceptance has the page open or closed while the task closes.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §2: 'The server re-derives its data on a fixed tick, hashes the result, and pushes it to the page ... only when the hash changed' and '`tp epic export` gains ...: `revision` (a hash of the payload's inputs) and `generated_at`' and acceptance 'an unchanged repository pushes nothing after the first state'.
finding: The server 'hashes the result, and pushes it ... only when the hash changed', but the same section adds `generated_at` to the export payload the page reads. A hash of the result that includes `generated_at` changes on every tick, so the acceptance 'an unchanged repository pushes nothing after the first state' fails; an implementation that hashes `revision` instead passes. Two correct readings disagree on whether the push happens.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 1 (§2 push hash vs generated_at), fixed by the same repair.

suggestion: Say what the push compares: the payload with `generated_at` excluded, or `revision` plus an equivalent input hash for the `tp export` side, which carries no `revision`.

evidence: §2 line 51: "The server re-derives its data on a fixed tick, hashes the result, and pushes it to the page ... only when the hash changed"; line 61-62: "`tp epic export` gains ... `revision` (a hash of the payload's inputs) and `generated_at`"; acceptance line 76-77: "an unchanged repository pushes nothing after the first state."
finding: The server pushes 'only when the hash changed', hashing 'the result', and the result is the export payload, which now carries `generated_at`. Hashed literally, every tick changes the hash and the server pushes on every tick, failing the acceptance that an unchanged repository pushes nothing. The spec gives `revision` (a hash of the inputs) but does not say the push decision uses it or excludes `generated_at`.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 1 (§2 push hash vs generated_at), fixed by the same repair.

suggestion: Say the push decision compares the payload without `generated_at` (or compares `revision`, covering the `tp export` side too).

evidence: §4 lines 102-106: "A KPI strip opens the tab ... Then the lifecycle band (§6), the \"now\" lists ..., the map (§9), the chain of a selected epic ..., the milestone matrix, and plan review (§5)." vs §3 lines 88-90: "plan review comes first whenever no epic has a bound spec ... Once a spec is bound the lifecycle band leads and plan review follows the \"now\" lists." and line 97-98: "the first panel of the Epics tab is plan review."
finding: §3 and §4 give different panel orders for the Epics tab. §4 fixes one order (KPI strip, band, now lists, map, chain, matrix, plan review last) without conditions; §3 says plan review comes first when no spec is bound and otherwise 'follows the now lists', i.e. before the map. §3's acceptance also calls plan review 'the first panel' while §4 says the KPI strip opens the tab, leaving open whether the strip counts as a panel.

resolved.evidence: §3: plan review follows the KPI strip while no epic has a bound spec, and once one is bound the tab takes §4's order; the acceptance names the panel after the KPI strip.

suggestion: Write the order once, in §4, for both cases (no bound spec / some bound spec), and say whether the KPI strip stays above plan review in the planning case.

evidence: §5 line 127-128: "and each recorded round's finding count, total and by role, in round order"; §11 line 277-278: "`tp epic review <slice> --history` prints the slice's rounds, each with its findings by role".
finding: `--status` now prints every recorded round's finding count, as a total and by role, in round order. §11's `--history` prints exactly that per round. `--status` is the frequently polled call that answers 'what next for this slice' (state, grantable, stale cause, cap/grants). The per-round series only draws the convergence curve, and it grows with every round on every `--all` call.

resolved.evidence: §5: the per-round finding counts move out of --status into the export's slices[] (and §11's --history prints them); the acceptance now reads the export.

suggestion: Keep the per-round counts in `--history` and in the export's `slices[]` that the page reads, and leave them out of `--status`, or at least out of `--status --compact`.

evidence: §6 lines 151-152: "Epic stages (planned, claimed, specced, in progress, done) over spec phases (review to release), each a count of work epics"; §17 line 410-411: "the audit round that brought the last bound file to release"; §13 line 316 lists the steps "ground, review, decompose, implement, audit, release".
finding: The band counts work epics per spec phase, but an epic can have several bound files in different phases (§17 speaks of 'the last bound file'), and the band's phases run 'review to release' while a bound spec can be in ground. Whether an epic with two bound specs counts once (which phase?) or once per file, and where an epic whose spec is in ground counts, is unstated; two implementations will print different band counts.

resolved.evidence: §6: an epic with several bound specs counts once, at the earliest of their phases. The ground part does not apply: tp resume reports no ground phase (SKILL.md), so a grounding spec reads as review.

suggestion: Say which phase an epic with several bound files counts in (e.g. its least advanced file), and whether ground is a band phase.

evidence: spec/1.8.0.md §6: 'Epic stages (...) over spec phases (review to release), each a count of work epics'; §3: 'With task files and no graph it opens on Specs; the Epics tab stays, ... and its lifecycle band shows the spec phases alone.'
finding: §6 defines every band entry, spec phases included, as 'a count of work epics'. §3 says that with task files and no graph the band 'shows the spec phases alone'. With no graph there are no work epics, so every phase count is zero by §6's definition, unless the phases count task files, which §6 does not say. The spec also does not say which phase a work epic with several bound files in different phases counts under, or whether unbound files count at all when there is a graph.

resolved.evidence: §6: with no graph the spec-phase counts count task files (the no-graph band itself is operator-decided, dashboard.md §6 q6); the several-bound-files part is fixed with finding 15.

suggestion: State the unit of the spec-phase row: task files, bound and unbound, per phase. Or, if it counts epics, say which bound file's phase an epic counts under, and what the no-graph band counts.

evidence: §2 line 62: "a per-epic `layout` (§9)"; §9 line 217-218: "The layout is in the export (§2), so the same graph always draws the same way"; §16 line 385: "`--compact`, as everywhere in tp, drops explanatory and bulky fields and keeps what a decision needs" is defined only for `tp export`, and SKILL.md line 797 lists no `--compact` for `tp epic export`.
finding: Every `tp epic export` call now carries a per-epic `layout` (lane, column, order) for the whole graph, which can be several hundred epics in the field project. Only the page's drawing uses it. No agent decision reads a lane or a column, and the spec gives `tp epic export` no `--compact` that would strip it, so agents that read the export as their plan contract pay for drawing coordinates on every call.

resolved.evidence: Layout in the export is §2's decision: the page's data is the export, and a page-side layout is rejected as a second derivation (§9). Whether tp epic export --compact drops layout is detail the export-layout task settles in its acceptance under tp's --compact convention.

suggestion: Have `tp epic export --compact` drop `layout`. Alternatively, keep `layout` out of the agent-facing export and serve it only from the dashboard's in-process payload.

evidence: §9 l.212-216: "the longest chain of openings is the main lane, milestones that open beside it in the same column are parallel lanes, milestones with an empty `opens_after` (opened by their own trigger) sit in a lane of their own, and milestones nothing on the main chain waits for form a side lane." Counterexample: L2 has opens_after [], M3 and M4 open after L2 in sequence and form the longest chain — L2 is both main-lane and triggered-lane. REFERENCE.md l.1375 confirms `[]` is distinct from absent (a track's first milestone), so the overlap is real.
finding: The four lane rules overlap, so a milestone can satisfy two and implementations place it differently. A milestone with an empty `opens_after` can start the longest chain of openings (main lane) and also be 'opened by its own trigger' (triggered lane); a milestone that opens beside the main chain in the same column but that nothing on the main chain waits for is both a parallel lane and a side lane. The acceptance 'both are placed in the triggered lane' fails for an implementation that gives main-lane membership precedence when one of the two roots the longest chain.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 2 (§9 overlapping lane rules), fixed by the same repair.

suggestion: Give the rules a precedence order (e.g. triggered first, then main, then parallel, then side), or state that the main chain is computed over milestones whose opens_after is not empty.

resolved.evidence: Duplicate of finding 6 (§16 --list with an unreadable file), fixed by the same repair.
